results.summary: This Wokwi project is a placeholder that currently does nothing, as stated in its own documentation. The eight inputs and eight outputs are named only with letters a through p and have no described function. There is no way to test it and no external hardware is specified. The documentation is essentially empty, so no meaningful behaviour can be inferred.

This Wokwi design is described as a full adder, with inputs a through f and outputs labelled xor, or and non-inverted inputs. The pin names suggest a mix of XOR, OR and pass-through logic rather than a complete adder, and the description is only one line. The author states they do not know how to test it, and no external hardware beyond Wokwi is listed. Documentation is very thin, so the exact function cannot be confirmed.

This design is a workshop exercise that inverts even-numbered inputs and drives the result onto a seven-segment display. The eight inputs IN0 to IN7 map to the seven segment lines plus decimal point, and the description says it counts from 1 to 8. It is tested by observing which segments light up on the display. No external hardware is needed beyond the Tiny Tapeout board and its display, and it appears to be a teaching example.

This design prints five characters, four selected characters plus a newline, to a serial monitor. Input 6 feeds a multiplexer and input 7 enables serial output, which is transmitted on output 7 to the receiver pin of an Arduino. It is tested by setting the seventh and eighth input switches on and watching the Arduino serial monitor. The project requires an Arduino Uno as external hardware and runs at a low 300 Hz clock.

This project is a simple bank of inverters, with eight inputs in0 to in7 and eight outputs o0 to o7. The documentation says only that it contains inverters and wires, and testing is done by simulation. A seven-segment display is listed as external hardware, presumably to observe the inverted outputs. It is a basic educational logic design with minimal documentation.

This design is a calculator that adds numbers, using the input, bidirectional and output pins to enter and display values. It is tested by connecting a seven-segment display and eight input buttons. The documentation is extremely sparse, with every pin simply named a, so the exact encoding and arithmetic width are unclear. It appears to be a beginner exercise with little supporting detail.

This design combines AND, NAND and OR gates driven by inputs a and b, plus a chain of flip-flops that divide the clock by two at the 12th and 16th stages. It is tested by setting the inputs and checking the outputs against the expected gate truth table. The documentation includes a garbled truth table and admits the design does not really work as intended. No external hardware is listed, and the description is partly inconsistent with the pin names.

This project is explicitly incomplete, with the description, testing instructions and external hardware all marked as coming soon. The pins are named IN0 to IN7 and o1 to o8 but no function is described. Nothing about the intended behaviour can be determined from the available text. The documentation is effectively absent.

This design appears to be a single AND gate, with inputs IN0_AND and IN1_AND and output OUT0_AND. The documentation still contains the unfilled template text asking the author to explain how the project works and how to test it. No external hardware is listed and no test procedure is given. The only concrete information is the pin naming, so the design is inferred to be a basic AND gate.

This project implements four AND gates, each connected to a pair of inputs such as IN0 and IN1, with results on the corresponding outputs. It is tested by checking that each output matches the AND of its input pair. The design is a straightforward logic-gate exercise with no external hardware required. Documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the function.
